sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **New Industrial Policy (NIP) 1991**: Landmark policy announced on July 24, 1991, drastically reducing industrial licensing, opening up foreign direct investment (FDI), and redefining the role of the **public sector**.
• **Abolition of Industrial Licensing**: Licensing was abolished for almost all industries except 18 (later pruned down to 4: Defence electronics/aerospace, explosives, hazardous chemicals, and tobacco/cigars; subsequently reduced further to atomic energy and railway transport under exclusive public sector domain).
• **MRTP Act Amendment**: The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act was dismantled, removing asset-limit thresholds for large industrial houses and shifting focus from curbing monopoly to controlling **unfair trade practices** (later replaced by the Competition Act, 2002).
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Share of Manufacturing in GDP (targeted to reach 25% under the National Manufacturing Policy and Make in India initiative).

items.definition: Government permission required to set up, expand, or shift an industrial unit; drastically dismantled in 1991 to promote ease of business.

Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (1973), which treated all foreign exchange transactions as criminal offenses unless permitted, was replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act (1999), facilitating external trade and payments.
Introduction of Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) system, granting autonomy (Navratna, Maharatna, Miniratna statuses), and strategic disinvestment.
Narasimham Committee (financial sector), Abid Hussain Committee (small scale industries), and the Competition Act, 2002.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Industrial Corridors**: Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC), Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor (CBIC) leveraging the Dedicated Freight Corridors (DFCs).
• **Driving Advantages**: Multimodal connectivity, plug-and-play infrastructure, reduction in logistics costs, and agglomeration economies.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Stagnation of manufacturing share around 16-17% of GDP, regulatory compliance burdens, land acquisition hurdles, and infrastructure bottlenecks.
• **Policy Interventions**: PM GatiShakti, National Logistics Policy, PLI schemes across 14 sectors, and Make in India 2.0.

items.title: Mnemonic for 1991 Core Pillars
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'LPG' (Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Liberalization (removal of controls), Privatization (disinvestment/private entry), Globalization (integration with world economy through tariff cuts and FDI).
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly differentiates 1991 structural reforms from green revolution or banking nationalization.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Industrial licensing was reduced to 18 in 1991, 6 later, and currently stands at only 2 industries exclusively reserved for the public sector (Atomic Energy and Railway Transport).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often frames statements claiming that industrial licensing was completely abolished for all sectors in 1991. This is false; strategic, environmental, and safety-related sectors retained licensing requirements.

Mains Value Addition: Emphasize the transition from 'Jobless Growth' to 'Make in India' and integrating domestic manufacturing into Global Value Chains (GVCs) via PLI schemes and quality control orders (QCOs).

keyTakeaways: The 1991 Industrial Policy ended state monopoly and bureaucratic licensing, ushering in market-led growth.
Reforms extended beyond domestic deregulation to foreign investment inflows (FDI) and foreign exchange management (FEMA).
Contemporary industrial reforms focus on infrastructure integration (PM GatiShakti) and sector-specific incentives (PLI).
